nodes.label: Static hosting
nodes.one_line: Deploy a static site to a host from a repo and get a working public URL.
know_what: Static host — a platform (Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages) that serves pre-built files from a CDN, with no server-side runtime
Build command / output directory — the two settings a static host needs to know: how to build the site and where the built files land
Custom domain vs default subdomain — pointing a real domain at the host versus using its free generated subdomain, a DNS configuration step distinct from the deploy itself
Deploy trigger — what causes a new deploy (a git push, a manual trigger, a webhook), and confirming the trigger you expect is actually the one configured
Cache invalidation — a CDN serving a stale version of a file after a new deploy until its cache expires or is explicitly purged
know_how: Connect the repository to the host and configure the build command and output directory correctly before the first deploy
Confirm the deployed URL actually serves the latest commit, not a stale cached build
Set up a custom domain and verify DNS propagation before considering the deploy done
Check the deploy log for build warnings, not just a green 'deployed' status
Confirm the deploy trigger matches expectations (e.g. every push to main, not every push to every branch)
habits: Check the actual deployed URL after every deploy, not just the host's dashboard status
Read build logs even on a successful deploy, since warnings there often predict future failures
Verify the deploy trigger configuration explicitly rather than assuming the default matches intent
Hard-refresh or check in an incognito window when a deploy doesn't seem to reflect recent changes, to rule out caching
Recheck the live site after any change to build configuration, not just after a code change
nodes.checkpoint: Connect a repository to a static host, configure the build correctly, and get a live public URL that reflects the latest commit, verified by checking the deployed page directly.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming a 'deploy successful' status means the site is actually correct — a misconfigured build output directory can deploy successfully while serving an empty or stale page, and the failure is only visible by actually checking the live URL.

nodes.label: Environment config
nodes.one_line: Separate configuration and secrets from code using environment variables, correctly scoped per environment.
know_what: Environment variable — a value injected into the running app from outside the codebase, the standard way to keep config and secrets out of source
.env file — a local file holding environment variables for development, which must never be committed to version control
Environment-specific values — different values for the same variable name across local, staging, and production, and the risk of a value leaking from the wrong environment

Build-time vs runtime injection — a frontend value baked into the built bundle (visible to anyone) versus a backend value read at runtime (kept server-side), a distinction with real security consequences
Secret vs config — a value that must stay confidential (an API key) versus one that's just environment-specific but not sensitive (a base URL), treated with different handling
know_how: Add a real .env file to .gitignore before it's ever created, not after a secret has already been committed
Set environment variables in the hosting platform's dashboard or CLI for each environment separately
Check whether a frontend variable is build-time (baked into the bundle, effectively public) before putting anything sensitive in it
Use a .env.example file with placeholder values so the required variables are documented without leaking real ones
Verify the correct set of variables is present in each environment before considering a deploy configured
habits: Check .gitignore includes .env before the first commit of a new project
Scan git history for any accidentally committed secret if a .env file is ever found tracked
Never put a genuinely secret value in a frontend/build-time environment variable
Keep a .env.example file current as new variables are added
Verify environment variables are actually set in each deploy target, not just assumed from local .env
nodes.checkpoint: Given an app that needs a secret API key, configure it as a runtime (not build-time) environment variable, confirm it never appears in the built frontend bundle, and confirm .env is excluded from version control.
nodes.common_failure: Committing a working .env file to get a deploy working quickly, intending to remove it later — the secret is now in git history permanently, recoverable even after the file is deleted from a later commit.

nodes.label: CI pipeline
nodes.one_line: Set up a CI pipeline that runs tests and checks on every AI-assisted commit before it can merge.
know_what: CI pipeline — an automated sequence (install, lint, type-check, test, build) that runs on every push or pull request before a change can merge
Required check — a CI job configured to block merging when it fails, versus one that runs informationally without blocking
Pipeline speed vs coverage — a fast pipeline that only runs a subset of checks versus a thorough one that runs everything, and the tradeoff in feedback latency
Flaky CI job — a job that fails intermittently for reasons unrelated to the actual change, which erodes trust in the pipeline if not addressed
CI environment parity — running CI against a similar Node/language version and dependency lockfile as production, so a pipeline pass actually predicts a working deploy
know_how: Configure lint, type-check, and test as required checks that block merging on failure
Run the pipeline against the exact dependency lockfile committed to the repo, not a freshly resolved one
Investigate any newly flaky job immediately rather than letting 're-run until green' become the norm
Keep the pipeline fast enough that it doesn't discourage frequent small commits
Confirm a required check is actually configured as required in the repository's branch protection settings, not just present in the workflow file
habits: Check branch protection settings actually enforce the pipeline as required, not just that the workflow file exists
Investigate a newly failing or flaky job the same day, rather than re-running past it
Keep the pipeline's dependency versions pinned to match what's actually deployed
Watch pipeline run time creeping up over time as a signal to prune or parallelize
Treat a green pipeline as necessary, not sufficient, for merging — pair it with the review practices it doesn't replace
nodes.checkpoint: Given a repository with no CI, set up a pipeline that runs lint, type-check, and tests as required checks, and confirm a failing test actually blocks a pull request from being merged.
nodes.common_failure: Setting up a CI workflow file that runs the right checks but never configuring branch protection to require it — the pipeline runs and reports status, but nothing actually stops a failing change from being merged.

nodes.label: Rollback plan
nodes.one_line: Set up a deployment rollback path so a bad AI-assisted release can be reverted in minutes, not hours.
know_what: Rollback path — a concrete, tested way to return production to the last known-good deployed version, distinct from just having version control history
Deploy history — the hosting platform's record of prior deployed builds, which a rollback typically targets by redeploying a specific prior one
Database migration rollback risk — a code rollback that leaves the database schema ahead of what the reverted code expects, a common gap in an otherwise clean rollback plan
Rollback time — how long it actually takes from noticing a bad deploy to production serving the previous version, the number that matters during an incident
Feature flag as rollback alternative — disabling a feature via a flag instead of redeploying, faster for isolated features but not a substitute for a full deploy rollback
know_how: Identify and test the platform's actual rollback mechanism before it's needed in an incident, not during one
Check whether a given deploy included a database migration that a code rollback alone wouldn't undo
Measure how long a rollback actually takes end to end, from decision to production serving the old version
Keep the last few deploys readily redeployable rather than only ever the most recent one
Practice a rollback at least once outside of an actual incident, so the mechanism is trusted, not just assumed to work
habits: Know the exact rollback command or button before the first real incident, not during it
Check whether a migration in the current deploy would survive a code-only rollback
Treat a rollback that's never been tested as a rollback plan that doesn't actually exist yet
Keep rollback time as a tracked number, not a guess
Re-verify the rollback path still works after any change to the deploy pipeline or database migration process

know_why.claim: A rollback plan isn't real until it's been exercised at least once, before an incident.
know_why.because: A rollback mechanism that's only ever been read about, not used, routinely turns out to have a gap (a migration that doesn't roll back cleanly, a config value that isn't captured in the deploy history) that's only discovered under incident pressure, when discovering it is most expensive.
know_why.disputed_by: Some practitioners argue that for a small, low-traffic project, the setup cost of practicing rollbacks regularly isn't worth it compared to just redeploying a fixed-forward commit quickly when something breaks.
know_why.source: Site reliability engineering practice (Google SRE book — release engineering)

nodes.checkpoint: Deploy a small change, then execute an actual rollback to the prior version, measuring the time from decision to the old version serving live traffic.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming a rollback will work because the hosting platform advertises one-click rollback, without ever having tried it — the first real attempt, during an actual incident, is when a database migration mismatch or a missing environment variable in the old deploy surfaces.

nodes.label: Basic monitoring
nodes.one_line: Add logging and error tracking so a production failure surfaces as an alert instead of a user complaint.
know_what: Error tracker — a service (Sentry, Rollbar) that captures unhandled exceptions from production with stack traces and context, instead of relying on users to report bugs
Structured logging — logging with consistent fields (timestamp, request id, severity) that can be searched and filtered, versus unstructured print statements
Alert threshold — the specific condition (error rate above X%, response time above Y ms) that triggers a notification, tuned to avoid both silence and alert fatigue
Uptime check — an external probe that periodically confirms the app is reachable, catching a full outage that internal error tracking might miss if the app can't even respond
Signal vs noise — the practice of alerting only on conditions that need a response, since an alert that fires constantly for non-issues gets ignored like any other noise
know_how: Wire an error tracker into both frontend and backend so an unhandled exception anywhere surfaces automatically
Set an alert threshold specific enough to page for real problems without firing on routine noise
Add an external uptime check independent of the app's own error tracking, so a full outage is still caught
Test the alerting path end to end by triggering a deliberate error and confirming a notification actually arrives
Review captured errors periodically even when no alert fired, since low-severity errors can still indicate a real problem
habits: Trigger a deliberate test error after setting up monitoring to confirm the whole alert path actually works
Check the error tracker's dashboard periodically, not only when an alert fires
Tune alert thresholds down when they're too noisy rather than letting them get ignored
Treat a service with no monitoring configured as not actually deployed yet, not just an item for later
Review a new alert's context (stack trace, request data) before acting rather than reacting to the alert title alone
nodes.checkpoint: Set up an error tracker and an uptime check for a deployed app, trigger a deliberate error, and confirm a notification arrives with enough context (stack trace, request info) to start debugging without reproducing it locally first.
nodes.common_failure: Deploying monitoring tooling but never testing that it actually alerts — a misconfigured integration (wrong project key, alert rule that never matches) can sit silently broken for months, discovered only when an incident happens and no one was notified.
sources: Google SRE book — monitoring distributed systems

nodes.label: Secrets rotation
nodes.one_line: Manage and rotate production secrets and credentials without an AI session ever seeing or logging them directly.
know_what: Secret rotation — periodically replacing a credential (API key, database password) with a new one, limiting how long a leaked secret stays useful if compromised
Secrets manager — a dedicated service (platform-native secrets, Doppler, Vault) for storing and injecting secrets, distinct from plain environment variables checked into a dashboard by hand
Blast radius of a leaked secret — what a compromised credential actually grants access to, which should be scoped as narrowly as possible per secret rather than one broad key used everywhere
Zero-downtime rotation — rotating a secret without an outage, usually by supporting both old and new values briefly during the transition
Secret exposure in logs or AI sessions — a credential accidentally printed to logs, error messages, or pasted into an AI chat session, a real and easy-to-miss leak path
know_how: Scope each secret narrowly to what it actually needs access to, rather than reusing one broad credential everywhere
Rotate a secret on a schedule or immediately after any suspected exposure, not only after a confirmed breach
Support both the old and new value briefly during a rotation so in-flight requests don't fail
Check logs and error messages for accidentally leaked secret values before considering a service production-ready
Never paste a real secret value into an AI chat session; use a placeholder and swap it in locally instead
habits: Treat any secret pasted into a chat session, even accidentally, as compromised and due for rotation
Scope new secrets as narrowly as the service allows from the moment they're created
Check logging output periodically for accidentally leaked credential values
Rotate a secret immediately on any suspicion of exposure rather than waiting for confirmation
Keep an inventory of which secrets exist and what they grant access to, so a rotation after exposure is fast, not a scramble
nodes.checkpoint: Given a service with one broad database credential, scope it down to a narrower role-based credential and rotate it with zero downtime, verified by confirming in-flight requests don't fail during the transition.
nodes.common_failure: Pasting a real API key or database URL into an AI chat session for debugging convenience — even if the session is 'private', the secret should now be treated as exposed and rotated, a step that's easy to skip because nothing appears to break immediately.
